ranges.en: Mishnah holds that anyone may substitute, the substitution takes effect, and the substitutor is lashed.
Objection: the mishna seems to permit substitution ab initio, yet later says it is valid only after the fact.
Counter-challenge: if the mishna meant ab initio, the verse prohibiting substitution would contradict it.
Rav Yehuda reinterprets the mishna: everyone may consecrate by substitution, but the act is forbidden and lashes apply.
What does the word everyone serve to include?
It includes an inheritor, so the mishna does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
Baraita cited: an inheritor may lay hands and substitute, per Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.
What is the reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda's position?
He derives initial consecration from its end: an inheritor cannot lay hands, so also cannot substitute.
From where do we derive the halakha of laying hands itself?
The three occurrences of his offering exclude a gentile's, another's, and a father's offering.
Per Rabbi Meir, why is his offering not needed to include joint owners, given the third occurrence?
Rabbi Yehuda excludes joint owners because their offering is not singular to one person.
Alternatively, Rabbi Yehuda includes joint owners, deriving the gentile and other exclusions from one verse.
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir, who holds an inheritor may substitute?
The repeated verb hamer yamir includes the inheritor in the power of substitution.

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir derives the laying of hands from initial consecration: an inheritor who substitutes also lays hands on the offering.
According to Rabbi Yehuda, what does the repeated verb in the substitution verse teach?
It serves to include a woman in the power of substitution.
A baraita: the passage speaks only in the masculine, so a woman's inclusion is derived from the and-if phrasing.
According to Rabbi Meir, from where is a woman's inclusion derived?
Rabbi Yehuda does not interpret the and-if phrasing as significant, so he derives it differently.
Both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree the verse explicitly includes women, by conjunction or repetition.
Should one infer that without this inclusion, a woman's substitution would not be effective?
Objection: Rav Yehuda cited Rav that a woman is equated with a man in all Torah punishments.
Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael: the verse equates women with men for all Torah punishments, so the objection stands.
Why, then, is it necessary for the verse to include women in the substitution prohibition?
The equating statement covers punishments applying alike to individuals and the public, not this one, which differs.
A mishna teaches that the public and partners cannot effect substitution, so a woman might be exempt too.
The verse therefore teaches that a woman who performs substitution is in fact liable to lashes.
Rami bar Hama asks whether a minor can effect substitution, and what circumstances this involves.
Objection: a minor who cannot yet vow cannot consecrate, so the dilemma cannot concern him.
The dilemma concerns a minor who has reached the age of vows.
Do we say a minor can substitute since the Master said he consecrates by vow?
The verse yafli includes a discerning minor on the brink of adulthood, so his consecration takes effect.
Does a minor substitute since he can consecrate, or not, since he is not liable? Likewise for a gentile.
A baraita: the double ish includes gentiles in vows and gift offerings, so their consecration takes effect.
Or perhaps, since a gentile never reaches liability for punishments, his substitution does not consecrate.
Rava brings a baraita: gentile-consecrated animals cannot be substituted, per Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yosei is stringent in all cases, and limits Rabbi Shimon's leniency on misuse to altar offerings.
In any event, the baraita teaches that gentiles cannot render an animal a substitute.
Rami bar Hama does not raise the dilemma when a gentile consecrates for a gentile to atone.
When a gentile consecrates and a Jew atones, do we follow the consecrator or the one atoning?
Solve it by Rabbi Yohanan's ruling: the atoner can substitute as if he had consecrated, so the dilemma resolves.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan's ruling continues: for another person's offering, the benefit of the atonement belongs to the atoner.
Rami bar Hama distinguishes that case: the offering comes on behalf of the Jew, so the atoner's possession governs.
Here, where a gentile consecrated, must possession by a substitution-capable person run from start to finish? Teiku, unresolved.
The baraita: gentile-consecrated animals cannot benefit ab initio; misuse liability is absent, the benefit prohibition is rabbinic.
What is the reason?
Misuse is excluded by a verbal analogy to teruma, where the verse specifies the children of Israel and not gentiles.
The baraita continues: a gentile's consecrated animal does not incur liability for piggul, notar or impurity.
Leviticus 22:2 specifies the children of Israel's holy items, excluding gentile-consecrated offerings from the impurity prohibition.
Notar is excluded by verbal analogy to the word profane used in the impurity verse.
Piggul is excluded by verbal analogy between the word iniquity in piggul and in notar.
All these prohibitions apply only to Israel's offerings, and a gentile cannot effect substitution.
Leviticus 27:10 and the opening address to the children of Israel in 27:2 show substitution applies only to Israel.
A second formulation of the same halakha, sourced differently, also excludes gentiles from substitution.
What is the reason?
Substitution of animals is juxtaposed with the animal tithe and the grain tithe, which apply only to Israel.
Numbers 18:24 limits the grain tithe to the children of Israel, and the same holds for substitution.
A gentile cannot bring libations for an independent offering, but his burnt offering requires libations, per Rabbi Shimon.
Numbers 15:13 and 15:14 show that a gentile's burnt offering requires libations, not that it is exempt.
Rabbi Yosei is stringent in all these cases and applies the same status to offerings of gentiles.
What is the reason for Rabbi Yosei's position?
Leviticus 22:18 equates gentiles' vow offerings with those of Israel, so their consecration is the same.
The baraita's limit: the exemption from misuse applies to altar offerings, while Temple-maintenance items incur misuse liability.
What is the reason?
The teruma analogy applies only to inherent sanctity, not to Temple-maintenance items whose sanctity inheres in their value.
Rav Yehuda says Rav's principle: for any Torah prohibition, lashes apply only if one performed an action to transgress it.
Is it an established principle that a prohibition without an action is exempt, given that substitution is one?
The mishna teaches that one who substitutes incurs forty lashes, showing a prohibition without action is punished.
Rav could have said the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds lashes apply even for an omission prohibition.
The mishna's first clause, as explained, rejects Rabbi Yehuda's view, so the mishna cannot be read as his.
The tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehuda that lashes apply for an omission, but disagrees on inheritance matters.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's rule, transmitted through a chain: lashes for omission apply to oath, substitution and cursing by God's name, and to teruma before first fruits.
From where do we derive that one who takes an oath in God's name is flogged?
Rabbi Yohanan in Rabbi Meir's name: Exodus 20:7 implies the heavenly court punishes oath-taking in vain.

ranges.en: The heavenly court does not absolve the oath-taker, but the earthly court flogs him and thereby absolves him.
Rav Pappa objects to Abaye: then the verse must mean he can never be absolved at all.
Abaye replies that the verse distinguishes courts: heavenly court does not absolve, earthly court flogs and absolves.
We found the flogging of a vain oath; from where do we derive it for a false oath?
Rabbi Yohanan derives it from the doubled word in vain in Exodus 20:7, applying the extra instance to false oaths.
Rabbi Abbahu objects: what are the circumstances of a false oath under this explanation?
If the oath is not to eat and he ate, an action occurred; if he swore to eat and did not, is he flogged?
But it was stated that one who swears to eat a loaf today and does not eat is not flogged.
Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish both state a view on whether the oath-taker is flogged.
Rabbi Yohanan holds not flogged, since no action is involved and omission-prohibitions carry no lashes.
Resh Lakish holds not flogged, since the forewarning was uncertain, and no lashes follow an uncertain forewarning.
Rabbi Abbahu resolves: the case is an oath that he ate when he did not, or did not eat when he did, by speech alone.
Why does the verse include oaths about the past, but not oaths about the future, as liable to lashes?
Rava: the Torah explicitly includes false oaths as similar to vain oaths, so false oaths must pertain to the past.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rabbi Abbahu from a mishna.
The mishna: an oath not to eat a loaf, repeated, is one utterance, liable to lashes if intentional and to a sliding-scale offering if unwitting.
What does the limiting term this is the oath exclude, if not oaths about the past?
Rather it excludes the unwitting case, and the mishna follows Rabbi Yishmael, who holds lashes but no offering for the past.
But say the latter clause: an oath that a stone is gold is exempt from offering, so what does this is the oath exclude?
Does the limiting term not exclude oaths about the past, so one is not flogged there?
Rather it excludes the unwitting case, and the latter clause follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires an offering for the past.
But if the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael, the latter clause follows Rabbi Akiva, so the first clause must too.
The first clause excludes a future oath, and the mishna is in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, so neither clause contradicts Rabbi Abbahu.
Rabbi Yohanan tells the tanna not to list effecting substitution among omission-liable cases, since it is an act by speech.
From where do we derive that one who curses another using the name of God is flogged?
Deuteronomy 28:58-59 and 25:2 read the term vehifla as lashes, so cursing by God's name is flogged.
Why not say that one who utters a true oath is also flogged, as this shows insufficient fear of God?
Exodus 22:10 explicitly permits a bailee to swear in court, so a true oath is not punished.
The verse may mean only that the bailee appeases the owner and is exempt from payment, yet still be flogged.
Deuteronomy 6:13 indicates that a truthful oath using God's name is permitted.
Isn't that verse required as the source for Rav's halakha on oaths?
Rav Giddel in Rav's name: Psalms 119:106 derives that one may swear to fulfill the mitzvot.
Counter: another verse, Deuteronomy 10:20, already teaches that a truthful oath is permitted.
Why not say the verse refers to one who pronounces the name of Heaven in vain?
Cursing another using God's name is no less a sin than pronouncing it in vain, so if flogged for one, flogged for the other.
Difficult: one who pronounces God's name in vain is atoned by lashes, but one who also harms another should need more.

That verse is a positive command, and a warning must be stated as a prohibition.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina: one who separates teruma before first fruits is also flogged.

Exodus 22:28 says not to delay the fullness of the harvest, which is first fruits, and the outflow of the presses, which is teruma.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina disagree on whether one who separates teruma before first fruits is flogged.
It may be concluded Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina holds flogging, since he stated the teruma-first-fruits ruling as flogged.

Mishna Demai 7:6 on two baskets of untithed produce, where separating second tithe before first tithe in the other basket draws flogging per Rabbi Elazar.

ranges.en: Clarifies the earlier exemption: no lashes for omission-type prohibitions, and per Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina, teruma before first fruits is not flogged.

Rabbi Avin: the tithing-order case is rectifiable by a positive command, which excludes lashes; Numbers 18:29 shows the rectification.
Rav Dimi teaches that one is not flogged for a prohibition that a positive command can rectify.
Abaye objects: is it correct that no lashes apply to any rectifiable prohibition?
Substitution is rectifiable by a positive command, yet the mishna teaches that the substitutor is flogged.
Rav Dimi: substitution has two prohibitions but only one positive command, which cannot uproot both, so lashes apply.

A tanna dispute from the Paschal offering verse: a positive command after a prohibition exempts lashes, per Rabbi Yehuda.

By inference, Rabbi Yehuda holds lashes apply for a prohibition that involves no action.
If Rabbi Yaakov exempts for lack of action, what is the clause but burn with fire for?
It teaches that remnants of the Paschal offering are burned on the first weekday if the sixteenth falls on Shabbat, per the mishna.
Hizkiyya's school teaches the same halakha as a tradition.
What is the reason?
The double word morning provides a second morning for burning when the first falls on Shabbat or a festival.
Abaye: whatever the Torah says not to do, if one did it, the act is effective and the violator is flogged.

Rava: the act is not effective at all; one is flogged for transgressing the Merciful One's statement.

ranges.en: A baraita objects to Rava: an Israelite rapist who divorces his victim remarries her unflogged, apparently refuting him.

The Gemara asks what Abaye derives from the phrase all his days.
Without that phrase one might think divorce is a remediable prohibition and remarriage optional; the phrase teaches obligation.
The Gemara introduces a second version of the same discussion.
A second version of the baraita is raised against Abaye: the Israelite who divorces his victim remarries her, apparently refuting him.
Abaye replies that the case there differs, since the verse makes the obligation to remarry absolute.

The Gemara concludes that this mishna refutes Rava.

He cites Numbers 18:32, which describes bearing no sin for lifting up the best, to support this derivation.
If the teruma were not sanctified there would be no sin, so inferior-for-superior teruma is valid.

The Gemara concludes that the mishna refutes Abaye.
Abaye replies that the case there is different.

Without the phrase one might limit the prohibition to wine and oil; the verse extends it to wine and grain, which carry no flogging.

The Gemara concludes that this mishna refutes Abaye's view.

It teaches that a firstborn or tithe animal whose blood is mixed with other offerings' blood is still sacrificed on the altar.

He cites the Yom Kippur verse on the blood of the bull and the blood of the goat placed on the altar.

Rava holds the bloods were kept separate, following Rabbi Yonatan, who disagrees with Rabbi Yoshiya.

The Gemara concludes that this mishna refutes Abaye.

The Gemara objects to Rava from separating teruma before first fruits, which the verse forbids delaying.

Abaye argues that an egg rots and becomes dust, so the chick from it is no longer attributed to the hen.

Rava replies to Abaye that if the baraita is taught, it stands and he cannot dispute it.
Mishna: Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus rules that a kosher animal that suckled from a tereifa is disqualified.
Asks the reason, and whether fattening by a tereifa would parallel fattening on idolatrous vetches.
Rabbi Hanina Terita taught that the animal was fed warm milk daily and survives only from the tereifa, so it is disqualified.
Mishna: consecrated animals that became tereifot may not be redeemed to render them non-sacred, nor to feed to dogs.
Asks from where these matters are derived.
Cites Deuteronomy 12:15 and expounds it to show that consecrated animals may not be redeemed to feed dogs.
Gives another reading: benefit from consecrated animals is only from slaughter onward, implying redemption to feed dogs is allowed; the chapter closes.
Mishna: animals for the altar and items for Temple maintenance differ in substitution, and in liability for piggul, notar and impurity.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: offspring and milk of blemished altar animals are forbidden after redemption, and consecrated Temple-maintenance property differs in several respects.
States the principle that all altar-consecrated items render an animal exchanged for them a substitute.
Objects that birds consecrated for the altar do not render a substitute, as a mishna teaches.
Replies that the mishna's rule was taught only about animal offerings.
Objects that the offspring of an altar animal does not make a substitute, as a mishna teaches.
Explains that this mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the offspring does make a substitute.
Objects that a substitute itself is consecrated for the altar yet does not make a substitute.
Replies that the principle was taught only about the principal offering, not a substitute.
Concludes the mishna may follow the Rabbis, who hold offspring does not make a substitute.
Mishna: the Temple treasurer does not pay craftsmen from money designated for altar animals.
Asks from where it follows that Temple-maintenance consecrations are used to pay craftsmen.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Exodus 25:8 on building the Tabernacle, from which consecrated property may pay craftsmen.
Quotes the mishna: unspecified consecrations are for Temple maintenance and take effect on all items.
Asks which tanna holds this mishna's ruling.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yohanan that the mishna is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua.
Cites a baraita from Shekalim: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute how a donor's unspecified consecration of animals is handled.
States Rabbi Yehoshua's view that males are offered as burnt offerings and the rest goes to Temple maintenance.
Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that Rav holds that even Rabbi Eliezer concedes for an all-male herd.
Explains the dispute over a mixed herd through whether a person divides his vow, with Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua holding opposite views.
Gives another version by Rav Adda bar Ahava: when only the type of animal is specified, even Rabbi Eliezer agrees all are for the altar.
Explains that the dispute arises when other property is consecrated together with the animals, and the rulings on dividing a vow.
Asks how the mishna's wording fits each version of the explanation.
Cites a baraita with the same wording, that the money goes to Temple maintenance.
Mishna: consecration for Temple maintenance takes effect on all items, including those not usually consecrated.
Asks what the emphasis on all items is meant to add.
Ravina says it adds shavings and fallen leaves of a tree consecrated for Temple maintenance.
Mishna: one is liable for misuse of Temple-maintenance items and their by-products, but not altar by-products.
Asks what the exclusion of altar by-products is meant to add.
Rav Pappa says it adds the milk of altar animals and the eggs of pigeons.
Cites a baraita: milk of consecrated animals and eggs of pigeons may not be used, but misuse of them is not liable, unlike Temple-maintenance animals.
Explains that the altar rule applies to altar animals, while a hen consecrated for Temple maintenance creates liability for its eggs.
A female donkey consecrated for Temple maintenance creates liability for misuse of its milk.
Even the view that altar offspring can be misused applies only to by-products fit for the altar.
Explains that offspring fit for the altar can be misused, while those not fit, like eggs and milk, cannot.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: neither altar nor Temple-maintenance consecrations may change status, animals may be valued and dedicated to priests, and Rabbi Shimon differs on death.
Rav Huna rules that an altar animal dedicated to the priests has no effect.
Asks the reason for Rav Huna's ruling.
Cites Leviticus 27:28 that every devoted item that is most holy belongs to the Lord, not the priests.
Objects with a baraita that Temple-maintenance items and priestly dedications cannot be combined, implying an altar animal combined with a priestly dedication takes effect, refuting Rav Huna.
Rav Huna replies that the baraita is an incomplete case, and the altar-animal-to-Temple-maintenance case is the one that takes effect.
Objects that the altar-animal case should have been taught alongside the other cases in the baraita.
Explains the tanna taught only cases where two forbidden consecrations are involved, not the case with a single forbidden consecration.
Objects with a mishna that one who consecrates an altar animal's value must mean Temple maintenance, but then the wording question arises.
Explains that both clauses refer to Temple-maintenance consecrations, and the wording of consecration or dedication makes no difference.
Objects with two baraitas that teach an altar animal consecrated to the priests takes effect, refuting Rav Huna again.
Asks how the verse Rav Huna relies on should then be read.
Ulla reads Leviticus 27:28 to mean every dedicated item, so a priestly dedication applies even to altar animals.
Asks whether Ulla really said this, given his own opposing statement.
Cites Ulla's own ruling that an altar animal dedicated to Temple maintenance has only a delay effect, which seems to conflict.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Replies that the rule making a valued altar animal given to Temple maintenance liable is rabbinic, while Torah law requires only the treasurers' delay.
Asks why the verse on dedicated items is needed at all, since most holy already appears there and the misuse rules would follow.
Cites Rabbi Yannai and a baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: misuse is explicit only for burnt offerings, while other offerings' liability comes from the word all.
Asks why the verse is needed to include these offerings when most holy is already written.
Explains that even where most holy is written, a verse is still required to extend misuse liability to such offerings and dedications.
Ulla rules that a burnt offering consecrated to Temple maintenance has only the treasurers' delay, not a prohibition on slaughter.
Objects with a baraita that a burnt offering consecrated to Temple maintenance is prohibited to slaughter until redeemed.
Explains that the baraita speaks of the rabbinic rule, since its last clause says what he did stands, showing Torah law does not require redemption.
Asks whether the rabbinic reading fits the baraita's last clause on two counts of misuse, which would then need Torah-level consecration.
Explains the baraita means that if the valuation were by Torah law, the offering would be liable on two counts of misuse.
Mishna: Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis dispute whether dead consecrated animals may be redeemed, distinguishing altar and Temple-maintenance animals.
Rabbi Yohanan says that according to the Rabbis both kinds of consecrated animals fall under standing and valuation, so dead ones are buried.
Reish Lakish says that according to the Rabbis only Temple-maintenance animals fall under standing and valuation, while altar animals do not.
Both explanations agree that Rabbi Shimon includes only altar animals under standing and valuation, and a blemished-from-the-outset animal is always redeemable.
Objects that on Reish Lakish's reading Rabbi Shimon should have stated his ruling simply without specifying Temple-maintenance animals.
Reish Lakish replies that Rabbi Shimon was unsure whether the first tanna's ruling concerned altar or Temple-maintenance animals.
Cites a baraita agreeing with Rabbi Yohanan, using Leviticus 27 to show standing and valuation applies to blemished and non-kosher animals.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the verse on standing and valuation is establishing.
Cites Leviticus 27:11 and expounds it to show only blemished animals with a permanent blemish are redeemed, excluding temporary blemishes.
Concludes that the Merciful One ordains standing and valuation for a blemished animal.
Asks the reasoning of Reish Lakish, who holds that altar animals are excluded from standing and valuation.
Rav Giddel cites Rav: the verse says good or bad, and the word it excludes altar animals from the halakha.
Asks, on Rabbi Yohanan's view, what the word it is meant to exclude.
Objects that Levi's school includes even blemished-from-the-outset animals and all creatures, which conflicts with the word it excluding something.
Asks the reasoning of Rav Yehuda's account of Rabbi Shimon's view.
Explains that Rabbi Shimon's view follows from the verse distinguishing good from bad, so altar animals are included and Temple-maintenance animals excluded.
Asks why the verse would not then say between good and bad if the distinction were meant.
Cites a baraita: unblemished dead Temple-maintenance animals are buried, and Rabbi Shimon's version refutes Rabbi Yohanan's reading.
Rabbi Yohanan replies that the case is an animal blemished from the outset, which the Rabbis hold is redeemable.
Argues that the baraita must concern blemished-from-the-outset animals, since otherwise Rabbi Shimon would disagree with the Rabbis on altar animals too.
Objects that the baraita refutes Reish Lakish, and cites another baraita with Rabbi Shimon's distinctions that refutes Rabbi Yohanan.
Rabbi Yohanan replies that the baraita concerns blemished-from-the-outset animals, which avoids disagreement on altar animals.
Asks whether the baraita then refutes Reish Lakish, since Rabbi Shimon would not disagree on altar animals.
Reish Lakish replies that the baraita concerns consecration before blemish, and Rabbi Shimon does disagree about altar animals too.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira how Reish Lakish can say altar animals are excluded when a baraita teaches altar animals are included.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Suggests concluding from the baraita that sacrificial animals may be redeemed in order to feed them to dogs.
Rejects that inference: the baraita refers to animals that were slaughtered before redemption, not to natural death.
Cites a baraita: Rabbi Meir says slaughtered blemished sacrificial animals are buried, while the Rabbis say they are redeemed.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira why, on Rabbi Shimon's view, unblemished Temple-maintenance animals must be buried.
Rabbi Zeira replies that such animals are fit for the altar, citing a baraita that they may be redeemed only for the altar.
Asks whether Rabbi Yohanan and everyone agree that a blemished-from-the-outset animal is not included in standing and valuation.
Objects with a mishna in Bekhorot that such animals are not consecrated, are sold, and if they die may be redeemed.
Rav Yehuda explains that the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who includes altar animals in standing and valuation.
Gives the reasoning from the verse excluding blemished-from-the-outset animals, which Rabbi Shimon accepts and the Rabbis reject.
Asks who the Rabbis in that view are, and why the mishna would state only Rabbi Shimon's view if they agreed with him.
Abaye replies that Rav follows Reish Lakish, or alternatively that Rav follows Rabbi Yohanan, and the mishna follows the Rabbis.
Mishna: lists sacrificial items that are buried, including a miscarried fetus and placenta, and a stoned ox.
Rabbi Shimon says non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard are burned.
Mishna: lists items that are burned, including leavened bread on Passover, impure teruma, and sacrifices slaughtered out of time or place.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a provisional guilt offering and an uncertain bird sin offering are burned, though Rabbi Yehuda says they are buried.
Rabbi Yehuda says the uncertain bird offering is cast into the courtyard drain to its mother.
States the principle that items buried are not burned and items burned are not buried.
Rabbi Yehuda permits burning items meant for burial as a stringency, but the Rabbis reject changing the method of destruction.
Mishna: the hair of a nazirite is buried.
Tavi raises a contradiction from a mishna in Orla that a sack woven with nazirite or firstborn donkey hair is burned.
Rav Nahman resolves it: one mishna concerns an impure nazirite, the other a pure nazirite whose hair is burned.
Tavi objects that the firstborn donkey case still contradicts, since one mishna buries the hair and the other burns it.
Rav Nahman says nothing and asks whether Tavi has heard any other answer on the matter.
Tavi reports Rav Sheshet: the Orla mishna concerns hair woven into a sack, while the other concerns hair alone.
Other Sages give the same resolution: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Elazar each offer a version.
Rav Nahman objects that the sack should be nullified by the majority of its material.
Rav Pappa says the bird design is significant and not nullified, so the sack is burned.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whose view the mishna follows.
Rabbi Yirmeya says it follows Rabbi Yehuda, who allows burning as a stringency.
Rav Nahman objects that removing the design would make burning unnecessary, so Rabbi Yehuda's view should not be needed.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that if removal is impossible, the mishna is read as Rabbi Yehuda's view, as a third resolution.
Mishna: leavened bread on Passover is burned.
Explains the unattributed mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds leaven is removed only by burning.
Mishna: impure teruma and orla and vineyard seedlings are burned or buried depending on their nature.
Asks what counts as an item whose proper destruction is burning, or burial.
Explains that foods are destroyed by burning and liquids by burial.
Mishna: an uncertain bird sin offering is burned, while Rabbi Yehuda says it is cast into the drain.
Cites a baraita with Rabbi Yehuda's method of casting the bird limb by limb into the Kidron drain, with all buried items not burned.
Asks the reason buried items may not be burned.
Explains that buried items' ashes are prohibited, so burning them risks benefit from forbidden ashes.
Asks whether the blood of a menstruating woman and corpse flesh, dried and pure, are then permitted to derive benefit from.
Rav Pineḥas objects with a baraita that bird crop and feathers are removed from misuse, implying buried items are permitted.
Asks whether the ash of burned consecrated items is permitted, given a baraita that says it is prohibited forever.
Explains that an asherah can be nullified by a gentile, unlike consecrated property, so the baraita states them separately.
Rami bar Hama limits the permission to cases where the misuse itself changes the status, while an accidental fire leaves the ash prohibited.
Rav Shemaya says the baraita concerns removing the altar ashes, and that ash remains prohibited forever.
Cites Leviticus 6:3 on removing the altar ashes, showing they remain sanctified even after the item is burned.
Closing formulas for the chapter and for the tractate Temurah.
